analysis.one_liner: Requires federal approval of oil spill contingency plans and lets the government bar ships without them.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee: introduced in May 1989, it was referred to committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After oil spills, companies would have to file a detailed cleanup and prevention plan with the federal government — showing they have the money, equipment, and procedures to contain and remove a spill — and update it regularly. The federal government would review and approve those plans, charge the companies a fee to cover the review, and report to Congress on spill-prevention technology. If a ship or terminal operator didn't have a current approved plan, the government could keep that ship out of U.S. ports or block oil from moving through that terminal.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishermen, and tourism businesses whose waters and livelihoods are threatened by oil spills, and taxpayers who currently bear cleanup costs when companies are unprepared. The bill shifts spill-preparation responsibility and its costs onto the companies that move oil.

how_it_helps.text: Terminal and vessel operators would have to prepare local oil and hazardous substance discharge contingency plans and submit them to the President for approval on a regular basis, so a cleanup response exists before a spill happens rather than after [S2][S3].
Each plan must include proof of financial capability to carry it out, periodic testing, containment and removal procedures, and maintained equipment and supplies [S3].

In a spill, the President must oversee that the removal plan is properly implemented and protect natural resources, wildlife, and human life and health, taking into account comments from affected third parties [S3].

The President could deny a vessel entry to any U.S. port, or block oil from moving through a terminal, if the operator has no current approved contingency plan — a real penalty for being unprepared [S2][S3].
Review costs would be paid by the companies through a fee set by regulation, rather than by taxpayers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil vessel operators and marine terminal operators, who would bear the cost of writing, testing, and maintaining spill plans, proving financial capability, and paying federal review fees — and who could lose port access if they don't comply.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls directly on vessel and terminal operators, who would need to fund planning, equipment, testing, and financial-capability demonstrations for every area they operate in [S3].

The port-entry and terminal-movement denial power could halt oil transport for operators caught without a current approved plan, an economic cost that falls on the companies and potentially on fuel supply chains [S2][S3].
The bill is a narrow planning-and-review measure: it does not itself raise liability limits, fund cleanups, or require double-hulled ships, so it would not on its own prevent or pay for major spills.
Enforcement depends entirely on presidential regulations to define areas, requirements, and fees, leaving the strength of the program to future rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: it would have required companies to prove — in advance and in writing — that they can contain and clean up a spill, and given the government leverage to keep unprepared operators out of U.S. ports. The costs fall on the companies that transport oil, which is where an honest supporter would say they belong, though small operators could face disproportionate paperwork burdens. Its weakness is that it is a modest planning measure rather than a comprehensive spill law; notably, Congress did later enact the much broader Oil Pollution Act of 1990, which included many of these ideas plus liability and cleanup provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey introduced the bill on May 12, 1989 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The bill's action history ends there: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action before Congress adjourned on January 3, 1991 [S5].
It drew just one cosponsor, a single Senate Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil vessel and terminal operators, who avoided federal plan-approval requirements, review fees, and the threat of port bans. The public did eventually get broader protections through the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, but this bill itself died unnoticed.

for.name: Frank R. Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, introduced it in the Senate, and saw it referred to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or advanced the bill; it died in committee with no further action.

against.name: Oil shipping and petroleum industry
against.what_they_did: Widely reported to have opposed stringent new oil spill regulation during the post-Exxon Valdez debate; the bill's planning mandates, fees, and port bans would have fallen on vessel and terminal operators.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was the Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no recorded opposition appears in the record.

industries.industry: Oil vessel operators and oil transport shipping
industries.note: The bill would require them to write, test, finance, and maintain federal spill contingency plans and pay review fees, with port entry denied if they fail to keep a current approved plan. Those are real costs, but they put cleanup readiness where the spill risk is.
Terminals would face the same planning, financial-capability, and fee requirements, and oil could be barred from moving through a terminal without an approved plan.

industries.industry: Coastal fishing, tourism, and waterfront communities
industries.note: Communities whose livelihoods depend on uncontaminated waters would benefit from guaranteed, tested spill-response plans and federal oversight of cleanups, with comments from affected third parties required in reviews.
